paras: The lynching of Lewis Davis was the hanging of a jailed prisoner by a masked mob in Crawford County, Missouri, early on Sunday, September 23, 1888. Davis, awaiting trial for the murder of his neighbor David Miller, was taken from jail and hanged over the grave of Pat Wallace, whom a mob had lynched two years before. The papers dwelt on his fight in his cell, and the judge ordered a special grand jury.

According to the Globe-Democrat, Miller left home on January 2, 1888, to meet Davis; other versions said the two were going to town to pay their taxes. A week later his body was found shot in the head, pockets turned out, near the farm of Davis's brother Elliott. The papers said the bullet fitted a pistol found on Davis, who was arrested on January 7 and denied the crime from then on.

Davis was held six months in the St. Louis jail, which the Forrest City Times said was done to keep him from being mobbed. He was indicted for first-degree murder, and the Globe-Democrat wrote that one important witness had since died and another had left the state. His jury was chosen by Saturday, the day another jury acquitted Elbert Clonts of murdering his father. Two accounts suggested that verdict made the lynchers fear Davis would also go free.

Between 2 and 3 a.m. a runner warned the sheriff of a coming mob, and deputy R. P. Dunlap was sent to Judge Bland at the hotel. Masked men, about forty by the wire account, met the deputy and marched him back to the jail. The Globe-Democrat said residents who came into the street were ordered indoors at gunpoint. With tools from a blacksmith shop, the mob held the lone guard and spent an hour cutting through the iron doors.

Inside, Davis pulled his bedstead apart and held off two fellow prisoners who had been ordered to help open the cell. He asked them to have his brother take his body home for burial, then fought until overpowered and bound, protesting his innocence to the end. At 3 o'clock the mob left with him, guarding the streets so that no one could witness the hanging. Davis was hanged from an oak half a mile north of Steelville on the Cuba road, directly over Wallace's grave.

Judge Bland ordered a special grand jury of "representative men of the county" and said all violators of the law must be punished. None of the masked men could be identified, though the Forrest City Times reported suspicion that the leaders had also lynched Wallace. No report of the grand jury's findings, arrests or indictments appears in the coverage.

Most papers ran a wire dispatch datelined Cuba, Mo., September 24, from the Washington Evening Star that day to Kansas, Ohio and Kentucky papers into October. Headlines ranged from "Taken From Jail and Lynched" and "Murderer Lynched" to "Davis' Drop Into Eternity at the Hands of Missouri Lynchers" and "Swung from a Limb." A longer Globe-Democrat account datelined Midland ran in the New York Sun on September 30, and a condensed version appeared in Kansas weeklies as "A Missouri Lynching."

Coverage generally treated Davis's guilt as settled, and Carolina briefs called him "a large land proprietor, who murdered David Miller." The Forrest City Times headlined the "Brutal Work of a Mob" yet said there was no doubt Davis would have been convicted. The Globe-Democrat told the cell fight with evident sympathy but called Davis a murderer and an assassin, while recording that he had always asserted his innocence. No report named Davis's race, and the Portland Daily Press placed the lynching in "Cuba, Miss."

The wire put the mob at about forty, the Globe-Democrat at thirty, and the Audubon County Republican at fifty. The wire said the sheriff sent out his deputy, the Globe-Democrat that the sheriff was home in bed, and the Audubon paper that the mob captured the sheriff and jailer. Only the Audubon paper said Davis was shot through the arm. Datelines name Cuba, Midland and Steelville, but both main accounts place the jail at Steelville.

reader.title: Lynching of Lewis Davis
bases: A masked mob broke into the Crawford County jail, took the prisoner Lewis Davis, who was awaiting trial for murder, and hanged him from an oak tree (A2, A18, A19).

Thirty to fifty masked men, acting without any lawful authority, took Davis from jail and hanged him (A2, A15, A19); he was awaiting trial for the murder of David Miller, and two papers said the mob was spurred by a recent acquittal (A18, A19).
The wire dispatch (A2, A18) and the separate Globe-Democrat account from Midland (A6, A19) agree that a masked mob broke into the jail and hanged Davis over Wallace's grave.

accounts.label: Wire report (Cuba, Mo., Sept. 24)
accounts.gist: A runner warned the sheriff, his deputy was captured by about forty masked men, the jail door was cut down, and Davis was hanged over Wallace's grave; Judge Bland ordered a special grand jury.

accounts.label: Globe-Democrat (Midland, Sept. 23)
accounts.gist: Thirty masked men ordered townspeople indoors, spent an hour cutting the iron doors, fought Davis in his cell and left at 3 o'clock; the sheriff was at home in bed and the judge was ordered back.

accounts.label: Digest version (Audubon County Republican)
accounts.gist: Fifty masked men captured the sheriff and jailer; Davis knocked three lynchers senseless, wounded others and was shot through the arm.

framing.detail: Wire headlines such as 'Murderer Lynched' and 'Swung from a Limb. Missouri Lynchers Make Short Work of a Jailed Murderer' treat Davis as guilty.
The Forrest City Times headlined the 'Brutal Work of a Mob' and reported the better class discouraged mobs, yet said there was no doubt Davis would have been convicted.
The Globe-Democrat account narrated Davis's fight sympathetically but called him a murderer and an assassin.
Briefs stated as fact that Davis 'murdered David Miller'.
